---
title: "The If Statement"
unit: 2
cluster: "Making Decisions"
---

Programs often need to make decisions: run one part of the code when a
condition is met, and another part when it is not. Python uses the `if`
statement for this.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to:

* write an `if` statement
* use `else` for the case when the condition is false
* use `elif` to check more conditions
* write an `if` statement inside a function or a loop

## Writing an if statement

A student needs 35 marks to pass an exam. This code displays `pass` when the
marks are high enough:

```{python}
marks = 72

if marks >= 35:
    print("pass")
```

The first line of the `if` statement has three parts:

| Part | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `if` | starts the statement |
| `marks >= 35` | the condition |
| `:` | ends the first line |

A **condition** is an expression that is either true or false. The operator
`>=` means "greater than or equal to". The operators `>`, `<` and `<=` work in
the same way: greater than, less than, and less than or equal to.

The indented lines under the `if` are called a **block**. Here the block has
one line. The body of a `for` loop is a block too.

The condition `marks >= 35` is true because `72` is greater than `35`, so
Python runs the block.

Change `marks` to a value below `35` and run the same statement:

```{python}
marks = 20

if marks >= 35:
    print("pass")
```

Nothing is displayed. The condition is false, so Python skips the block.

## The indented block

A block can have more than one line. Indentation tells Python which lines are
in the block:

```{python}
marks = 72

if marks >= 35:
    print("pass")
    print("Well done")
print("Result recorded")
```

The first two `print()` calls are indented, so they are in the block. The last
`print()` is not indented. It is not part of the `if` statement.

Run the same code with marks that are too low:

```{python}
marks = 20

if marks >= 35:
    print("pass")
    print("Well done")
print("Result recorded")
```

Python skips both lines of the block together. The unindented line still
runs.

Use four spaces for the block, and give every line in the block the same
indentation. You do not have to type the spaces one by one. Press the `Tab`
key once: most editors, including JupyterLab, insert four spaces.

An `if` statement must have a block. If no line is indented under the `if`,
Python reports an error:

```python
if marks >= 35:
print("pass")
```

```text
IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'if' statement on line 1
```

## Choosing between two blocks

An `if` statement on its own does nothing when its condition is false. An
`else` part adds a second block, which runs in that case:

```{python}
marks = 20

if marks >= 35:
    print("pass")
else:
    print("fail")
```

The word `else` starts at the same position as `if`, has no condition, and
ends with a colon. Its block is indented in the same way.

Python runs exactly one of the two blocks. With `72` marks, it runs the first
block and skips the second:

```{python}
marks = 72

if marks >= 35:
    print("pass")
else:
    print("fail")
```

## Choosing among several blocks

Some decisions have more than two outcomes. An `elif` part adds another
condition and another block. The word `elif` is short for "else if":

```{python}
number = 42

if number < 10:
    print(number, "is a single-digit number")
elif number < 100:
    print(number, "is a two-digit number")
else:
    print(number, "is a big number")
```

Python checks the conditions from top to bottom:

1. `number < 10` is false, because `42` is not less than `10`. Python skips
   the first block.
2. `number < 100` is true. Python runs the second block.
3. Python skips the `else` block.

Python runs the block of the first condition that is true and then leaves the
`if` statement. It does not check the conditions below that one:

```{python}
number = 1

if number < 10:
    print(number, "is a single-digit number")
elif number < 100:
    print(number, "is a two-digit number")
else:
    print(number, "is a big number")
```

The number `1` is also less than `100`, but only one line is displayed. The
first condition was true, so Python never checked the second.

An `if` statement can have many `elif` parts. The `else` part is optional and
always comes last.

## Inside a function or a loop

An `if` statement can be written inside another block, such as the body of a
function or the body of a loop. It is indented with that block, and each of
its own blocks is indented once more.

This function checks any number it is given:

```{python}
def check_number(number):
    if number < 10:
        print(number, "is a single-digit number")
    elif number < 100:
        print(number, "is a two-digit number")
    else:
        print(number, "is a big number")
```

The code has two levels of indentation:

| Indentation | Lines | They are in |
|-------------|-------|-------------|
| none | `def` | no block |
| four spaces | `if`, `elif` and `else` | the function body |
| eight spaces | the three `print()` calls | a block of the `if` statement |

The `if` statement is indented by four spaces, so it is part of the function
body. Each block inside it is indented by four more spaces: a block inside a
block.

Every call runs the `if` statement again with a new value of `number`:

```{python}
check_number(1)
check_number(42)
check_number(500)
```

Each call runs one of the three blocks. With the `if` statement in a function,
we can try every outcome without editing the code.

The body of a loop works in the same way. This loop checks the marks of every
student in a class:

```{python}
class_marks = [72, 20, 35, 91]

for marks in class_marks:
    if marks >= 35:
        print(marks, "pass")
    else:
        print(marks, "fail")
```

The `if` statement is in the loop body, so it runs once for each element. On
each iteration, Python checks the condition with the new value of `marks` and
runs one of the two blocks.

## Practice

### Problem 1

Write down the complete output of this code. Then run it and check your answer.

```python
temperature = 25

if temperature < 20:
    print("cold")
    print("wear a jacket")
print("done")
```

### Problem 2

Write a program that displays the words in this sentence that are longer than
five letters.

```python
sentence = "Python makes simple programs easy to write and pleasant to read"
```

The expected output is:

```text
Python
simple
programs
pleasant
```

### Problem 3

An electricity bill depends on the number of units used.

| Units | Price of each unit |
|-------|--------------------|
| the first 100 units | ₹3 |
| the next 100 units | ₹5 |
| every unit after that | ₹8 |

Write a program that displays the bill for the number of units below.

```python
units = 80
```

Check your program with these values:

| Units | Bill |
|-------|------|
| 80 | 240 |
| 150 | 550 |
| 250 | 1200 |

## Summary

An `if` statement checks a condition and runs a block of code only when the
condition is true. Indentation decides which lines are in the block.

| Form or rule | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| `if marks >= 35:` | starts an `if` statement with the condition `marks >= 35` |
| a condition | an expression that is either true or false |
| `marks >= 35` | true when `marks` is greater than or equal to `35` |
| `>`, `<`, `<=` | greater than, less than, less than or equal to |
| a block | the indented lines under `if`, `elif` or `else` |
| the block under `if` | runs only when the condition is true |
| `else:` | starts the block that runs when no condition above it is true |
| `elif number < 100:` | checks another condition when the conditions above it are false |
| `if`, `elif`, `else` | Python runs the block of the first true condition and skips the rest |
| an unindented line after the statement | runs whether the condition is true or false |
| an `if` statement inside a function or a loop | is indented once; its blocks are indented twice |
